Where it began

Chris Cairns was born on 13 June 1970 in Picton. Cricket ran in the family: his father, Lance Cairns, played for New Zealand before him. Chris was picked for the 1988 Youth World Cup, the first edition of what became the Under-19 World Cup, and that same year began a long stay with Nottinghamshire in English county cricket.

At home he played for Northern Districts and then, from 1990–91, for Canterbury, and he turned out for Northland in the Hawke Cup as well. His Test debut came against Australia on 24 November 1989, when he was 19.

The player

He played 62 Tests between 1989 and 2004, scoring 3,320 runs at 33.54 with five hundreds and 22 fifties. With the ball he took 218 wickets at 29.40, with five in an innings 13 times. His best, seven for 27, came against the West Indies in 1999. He needed only 58 Tests to complete 3,000 runs and 200 wickets, and only Ian Botham and Kapil Dev got there quicker.

His 158 against South Africa in 2004 came from just 172 balls. In one-day cricket his finest hour came in Kenya, in the 2000 ICC KnockOut Trophy final. His unbeaten 102 beat India and brought New Zealand its first major ICC title, and he was named player of the final.

What made him special

With the bat he hit hard and straight, and he loved a six. In a Test at Wellington in 2000 he sent several over the boundary of the Basin Reserve and into the street outside, and Shane Warne was taken off. For a time his 87 Test sixes were a world record.

With the ball he was a clever fast-medium bowler, and later he leaned on a slower ball that was very hard to pick. At Lord's one England batsman ducked under it, sure it was a beamer, and was bowled. He played 62 Tests, fewer than his talent deserved, and he is widely counted among the finest all-rounders the game has produced.

Away from the middle

He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and in the 2005 Queen's Birthday Honours he was appointed to the New Zealand Order of Merit, as an Officer, for his service to the game. He also played for an ICC World XI in the Tsunami Appeal match at the MCG, making 69 from 47 balls and adding 91 with his captain, Ricky Ponting. When he retired, the New Zealand Herald set him alongside Michael Jordan and Björn Borg.

In 2006 he set up a foundation to promote rail safety, and in 2008 he walked 1,001 kilometres to spread the message. He later made his home in Canberra, where he played club cricket for the North Canberra Gungahlin Eagles in 2011–12.

And finally

His last game for New Zealand was a Twenty20 match against the West Indies in February 2006, which included a bowl-out. The man with 218 Test wickets missed the stumps with both of his attempts. Cricket has a way of keeping even its best players humble.
